speechtext:
I had not thought of
carrying on the debate to-day, but since it has been carried on I hope I may be allowed to say a few words before asking the house to permit the withdrawal of the motion. It is apparent that there is peace and peace, because with some of the sentiments which have been expressed to-day I find myself in very strong opposition. If they were peace speeches that is not the sort of peace I am seeking. I was almost alarmed on Monday when all the parties in this house were endorsing almost everything in the resolution; I thought times had changed, but I feel more at home to-day.
While we believe we are always right and while we have a superiority complex that nothing can puncture, there is no use talking peace. Of course that goes to show that we should have a department which will try to teach us the truth with regard to our own position. I respect the mentality and the views, or at least the views, of everyone in this house, but I certainly do not understand how they arrive at some of their conclusions. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) dragged in the Crimean war, perhaps unhappily. I believe it was Lord Salisbury of England who said long after the Crimean war that England had backed the wrong horse. I suppose a lot of people died because England backed the wrong horse, but if anyone had said so at the time there would have been a great hullabaloo; they would have been unpatriotic. The hon. member also said that on this subject women have different views from men; I hope to heaven he is right. That should be a good argument why the women of his province should be given the franchise. Half the people of

International Peace-Miss Macphail
Canada are women and there seems no good reason why the voice of the women in regard to peace and war should not be expressed in this house, and also through the actions of the government. We do believe that women have a different point of view in regard to war; women place human life on a higher plane than men have placed it in the past, because women have suffered more that life may be.
I want to say just a word with regard to the statement made by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), who dealt with what I thought about the boys who went overseas. I can say what I think; I will not ask the hon. member to interpret my mind for me. I will take second place to no one in the respect, the honour and the love I hold for the boys who willingly sacrificed themselves between 1914 and 1918, and I want the sacrifice they made to be crystallized into such action as will prevent the same thing happening again. I certainly do not intend to reflect upon the men themselves or upon their relatives and friends, whose hearts were torn and bleeding and who naturally sought to do the thing that has always been done when they commemorated in marble and stone the brave acts of the men of this country. If that were all they did I should wholly agree with it, but other than that I cannot qualify the statement which I made the other day. I believe I spoke the truth, although others may not so believe.
Then for a moment I would like to refer to the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I am wondering to-day how he likes the company he is in. Everyone who spoke to-day considered that the Prime Minister made a very good speech. I have heard him make good speeches, but I did not consider that to be one of them. The statement of the government, through the Minister of National Defence and the Prime Minister, is something like this: "We want security, and we are trying to win it in two ways; through education, which we leave to all the departments, and through military preparedness, which we carefully organize and put under the direction of one of the ablest men, if not the most able man, in the cabinet. But the idea that security can be obtained by wiping out suspicion, fear, and ignorance we leave to everybody, and what is everybody's business will be well done." That was the argument advanced by those gentlemen. The Prime Minister said my view was narrow, that I should not have asked for a department to promote peace because that was a narrow or limited view. The Prime Minister's idea that all the departments will promote peace is so broad that it is flat. The Prime Minister is a sensible and clever man, and he knows as well as I do that what is left to all the departments will not be done by any. He might have said equally well, "Why have a department of Justice?" Surely the Prime Minister is not going to say that all the departments of the government are not striving for law and order. If that is the case, why have a Department of Justice with a minister at its head?

speechtext:
What is the Department of Justice for? We have a department for law and order. I would say that the spirit of the government is in favour of law and order, so why have that department? All the departments are interested in agriculture, especially at election time, yet we have a department to promote the welfare of agriculture. All the departments are interested in labour, yet we have a Department of Labour. I am afraid that argument does not hold water.
The Prime Minister also stated that I said I would be satisfied if the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) were at the head of the department suggested, and he asked if I realized that he would be bound by the solidarity of the government. If the Prime Minister reads my speech he will find that I said I would be satisfied to have the Minister of Justice at the head of this department if he were free of the cabinet; I was not taking a chance in the world.
For military preparedness we will spend
818.000.	000 this year; for the League of Nations $2,000 and for the Inter-parliamentary Union about $200, or some such small amount. We will spend a total of $2,200 for peace, the thing which is everybody's business, in support of which 245 members raise their voices while they give their votes and influence for military preparedness and the security obtained in that way. I am going to suggest to the Prime Minister again, and to the government, that they listen to the suggestion made by the member- for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) that we would be satisfied for the time being if one hundredth part of the amount that is spent for military preparedness this year be expended in promoting international peace and good will. That would give us this year the sum of
818.000.	. Then if someone were placed in
1794	COMMONS
International Peace-Miss Macphail
charge of the expenditure of that sum of money who really believe in the idea of achieving security through better international understanding, very much could be accomplished even during the present year. Some of the statements made in the house to-day, as well as some that were uttered on Monday, make me think that a deep knowledge of the causes of war and of the part the nations of the world have played in bringing about war, is very much needed in Canada. It certainly is not true that our cause is always right. If it were we never could go wrong, and we need never worry. But it is not true, it cannot be true, that an individual is always right. The same is true of some gentlemen to my right who have spoken to-day-they are not always right. Neither can a nation be always right. Why do we not look at this matter in a commonsense sort of way?
I enjoyed the address of the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart). It was a very kindly address, and in it the hon. member said that the schools are promoting peace. I wish that statement were true. I do not think it could be true unless our schools had most exceptional teachers. The text books at present in use do not tend to promote peace. During the last half dozen years the churches have been awakening to the importance of this matter and I think they are now striving to promote peace. But until we can get the people in the several provinces of Canada to demand from their governments that the text books used in the schools be absolutely fair, I do not believe the cause of peace will advance very far. If only the Dominion government were willing -they are not at the moment, and in the present temper of the house I am not sure that I want them to set up a department- but if they were willing set up a department to promote peace energetically, we could make a great advance in the desired direction. Soon we should have action on the part of the provincial governments to see that the text books used in the schools are absolutely fair and impartial and that the statements they contain are absolutely accurate.
We have had, I believe, a valuable discussion and it has done some good. It has disclosed that we do not all look at the question of peace in the same light and it also denotes that public opinion in this country is pretty strongly in favour of peace. Had this resolution been introduced seven or even five years ago, I fancy it would not have been met in the same kind manner that it has now. I ask to be allowed to withdraw

the motion, hoping that in the recess the government may see fit to set up some agency, possibly in the Department of External Affairs, to acquaint the people of Canada with the steps which they have taken to bring about international peace and good will. Even these facts are not known to the Canadian people. If the government do not see fit to do anything in the direction indicated between now and next session, the question can be reintroduced in some other form.

speechtext:
At this late stage in the
afternoon I would not have thought of proceeding with this motion were it not for the fact that I do not expect to be here when the next private members' day comes, and consequently my motion would go off the order paper altogether, so that I should not have an opportunity of presenting what seems to me to be a most important resolution, because if we were able to have a proper discussion, indeed if I had only half an hour to speak, I think I could show that there is a necessity for taking action and for amending our law in this regard. In the nature of the case I must shorten my speech very materially. I wish it to be understood in the first place that I am not dealing with the question of corporal punishment as such. I am neither supporting nor opposing the idea of inflicting the lash. I want the house to fix their attention entirely upon the one point and that is that when the lash is administered as a part of the penalty,, the full penalty of the lash should

be administered at the beginning rather than at the close of the sentence. This was brought to my notice because of an item that appeared in a newspaper last fall. The item reads:
Convicted of holding up and robbing a branch of the Bank of Nova Scotia at Campbellville, Ontario, last month while under arms, and stealing $1,100. Jack Walker, Arthur Williams and Clarence Thomas were to-day sentenced to 15 years in the Portsmouth penitentiary. For participation in the same crime, William Duncan was given 10 years in the penitentiary.
The men, who are all from Toronto, will, with the exception of Walker, receive 20 lashes. Ten of these will be given one month after they enter the prison, and the other ten one month before the expiration of their sentence. Walker, who has already been sentenced to 40 lashes in connection with another robbery, will not be lashed.
I am not objecting to the idea that is held that society should protect itself from the criminally minded. Society owes it to itself to protect itself from the criminal, but that idea is not inconsistent with the idea tha we should do all that lies in our power to reform the criminal, to make him again a useful member of society. There is one class of effenders against which we have decreed, whether rightly or wrongly, that we can protect ourselves only by taking away the life of the criminal. That is a subject all by itself that I will not deal with. There is another class that it has been thought we can protect ourselves against only by shutting them up for the period of their natural lives. These are important matters to deal with but they are not the subject of our immediate discussion.
If we put aside these classes and those offences for which a monetary fine is deemed adequate penalty, there remains that large class of offences that are punished by a term of imprisonment longer or shorter, with or without hard labour, and with or without corporal punishment. From one point of view it is more important that we should have a proper method of dealing with this class than with the others for the reason that, having paid the penalty for their offences, they are again returned to society. It is a matter of primary importance to us that these men who are again returned to society, if they are to become good citizens, if they are again to occupy useful places in the community, should come back to us in an attitude of mind that will lead them to feel that society is their friend and not their enemy. That is all-important, and therefore I wish to emphasize that aspect of the question-the welfare of society. I am not unmindful of the interests of the individual. I am not unmindful of the tragic conse-

quences to the human being who gives himself to a life of crime. I am not unmindful of the duty of the state to co-operate as far as possible with all those other agencies that are seeking to bring about the reformation of the criminal. But when we look at the matter from the standpoint of society, or of the individual, what folly it is to pursue a course that is calculated to nullify all the influences that are brought to bear upon a man during the time of his imprisonment and turn him out again upon society worse than when he went in!
I have been looking up the Auditor-General's reports, and I find that we spend large sums of money annually on our penitentiaries. We spend money for chaplains, trade instructors, teachers of various kinds. That is a - very proper expenditure; but again I ask: Is it not folly for us to spend money in an endeavour to promote the moral and spiritual welfare of the prisoner and then follow a course that is calculated to nullify all those influences? The fact that we spend that money constitutes on our part a recognition that we have obligations to the prisoner and to society. We may be under an obligation to visit retribution on the prisoner, but we are under an obligation to seek to bring about his reform so that he can again become a useful citizen. When a man is sen, tenced to a long term of imprisonment, with the lash if you like, and when that penalty is inflicted upon him at the beginning of the imprisonment, I can understand there is a possibility of that man coming to a sense of the error of his ways. Yes, Mr. Speaker, with all reverence I can understand such a man saying: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before Thee", and I can understand the possibility, during his term of imprisonment, of his yielding to the influences that are brought to bear upon him when he knows that he has already endured and suffered the penalty that was imposed upon him. But can anyone who has given a moment's thought to the matter believe that it is possible for a man to respond to any influences for good when he has that sentence hanging over him? He must go out from prison embittered. He feels that his hand is against every man and every man's hand is against him, or that every man's hand is against him and therefore his hand is against every man. It is not long before he comes into contact with criminal associates; he commits a burglarly; he goes armed although he does not intend to commit murder, but he is prepared to commit murder if necessary to accomplish his purpose and the end of the tragedy is the scaffold.

Alhabaska Election-Mr. Garland (Bow River)

speechtext:
No. I have only a few minutes to speak. I have had to shorten my speech very much already. I said that such a man must go out embittered in his whole attitude towards society. I have discussed this matter with a number of people who have expressed themselves in hearty sympathy with the proposal I have made. Indeed I have not heard a single dissenting word. I took the matter up with the -chaplain of one of our penitentiaries, and he expressed himself as in perfect accord with me, and gave me two other reasons why we should adopt the course that I am now urging. One was that the presence of such a prisoner in a penal institution was a menace to the well-being of the institution; his whole attitude was a menace. He so feared the punishment of the laslh that he was prepared to do anything to escape that penalty, and consequently was always looking for a way of escape, with danger to the guards. The other reason he gave me was this. He pointed out to me that by good conduct a prisoner might be granted as much as ten days in a month off his sentence. You see then the absurdity of sayin-g to a prisoner, "If your conduct is good, you will be released sooner, but at the same time that will bring you just that much nearer the time when the remainder of the penalty of the lash will be inflicted on you." I think it is absolutely absurd.
I should like to have quoted from the Winnipeg Tribune, which took notice of my motion when it was first put on the order papeT, and in which Mr. Justice Fullerton and Mr. Justice Stubbs expressed themselves as in favour of the principle I am advocating. The particular case that brought this matter to my attention was an appeal in which the judge sustained the sentence of imprisonment, but reversed that part of the sentence that inflicted the lash at the end of the term of imprisonment, and he expressed himself in very strong terms as disapproving of the lash.
I regret, Mr. Speaker, that circumstances have compelled me to omit much thait I wished to say. I think that a great many things were said in -the previous discussion which might just as well have been left unsaid, but before I sit down I am going to ask the Minister of Justice to consider the matter very seriously, and even at this late date to bring in an amendment to the criminal code
that will give effect to the purpose I have in view. I am sorry that under the circumstances I can do no more than I have done. The fault is not mine, but that of a large number of previous speakers who spoke at considerable length.

At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
